title: Introduction to the Letter to Philemon
subtitle: A guide to the writer, setting, household, and enduring message of the brief letter in which Paul sends a returning slave home as a beloved brother.

blocks.text: The letter opens with the name of Paul, who calls himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and it closes with his own pledge written by his own hand. Few writings of the New Testament have so secure a claim to their stated author. Christian teachers of the second century already counted Philemon among Paul’s letters, it appears in the earliest surviving lists of apostolic writings, and even those who in later centuries questioned other letters bearing Paul’s name have almost always left this one standing.

The character of the letter is its own best witness. It has no doctrinal controversy to settle and no church order to establish, so there would be little reason for anyone to compose it under an apostle’s name. A forger seeking authority for a cause would hardly invent a short appeal about a single slave, filled with private names, a request for a guest room, and a promissory note. The warmth, the wordplay on the name Onesimus, and the delicate tact of the request all carry the stamp of a real man writing to a real friend.

The letter also fits closely with Colossians. The same companions surround Paul in both, Timothy is named with him in both openings, Archippus is addressed in both, and Onesimus is mentioned in both as returning to Colossae. These overlapping details were never arranged to prove a point; they simply reflect one moment in Paul’s life when he wrote to a congregation and to one of its households at once. The two letters confirm each other, and together they give a rare picture of how an apostle cared for a church and for a single home within it.

Some early readers wondered whether so personal a note belonged in Scripture at all, since it seemed to deal with small private business. The church kept it, and rightly so. The letter shows the gospel at work in the ordinary fabric of life, where faith must decide how a wronged master will treat the one who wronged him. Its place in the canon reminds every generation that the grace of God reaches into kitchens, ledgers, and family quarrels as surely as into councils and creeds.

Paul writes in chains. He names himself a prisoner in the first verse, again in the ninth, and speaks of Onesimus as begotten in his bonds. Epaphras is described as his fellow prisoner, and Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke are with him. The question is where this imprisonment took place. Acts records Paul held for two years at Caesarea and then for two years at Rome, and some have proposed an unrecorded confinement at Ephesus, which lay much closer to Colossae.

The Roman setting best explains the evidence. During his house arrest there Paul lived in rented lodgings under guard, received visitors freely, and kept a circle of coworkers near him, which matches the gathering of companions named in the letter. Luke was with him on the voyage to Rome, and the great city was exactly the kind of place where a fugitive might hope to disappear among the crowds. The distance from Colossae is considerable, yet travel along the roads and sea lanes of the empire made such a journey quite possible for a determined man.

Paul’s request that Philemon prepare lodging for him shows that he expected to be released before long, a hope he expresses also in Philippians. On this reading the letter was written around A.D. 60 to 62, during the two years with which Acts closes, and was carried to Colossae by Tychicus together with the letter to the Colossians. The timeline below traces the path that brought Paul to that place and the hope he held while he wrote.

blocks.title: From Ephesus to a Roman Lodging
blocks.note: Dates are approximate, and the placement of Philemon in the first Roman imprisonment is the most probable reconstruction rather than a certainty.

events.title: Ministry at Ephesus
events.description: Paul teaches for more than two years at Ephesus, and the word of the Lord spreads through the province of Asia, reaching the Lycus Valley through Epaphras.

events.title: Philemon Comes to Faith
events.description: Philemon is converted through Paul’s ministry, most likely during a visit to Ephesus, and later opens his home at Colossae to the church.

events.title: Arrest in Jerusalem
events.description: After bringing the collection for the poor saints, Paul is seized in the temple and taken into Roman custody.

events.title: Detention at Caesarea
events.description: Paul is held for two years under Felix and then Festus, and finally appeals to Caesar as a Roman citizen.

events.title: Voyage and Shipwreck
events.description: Sailing for Rome under guard, Paul is shipwrecked on Malta and reaches the capital the following spring.

events.title: Onesimus Meets Paul in Rome
events.description: Living under guard in rented lodgings, Paul receives the runaway Onesimus, who believes and begins to serve him in the gospel.

events.title: The Letter Sent to Colossae
events.description: Tychicus and Onesimus carry Philemon and Colossians east, while Paul asks Philemon to prepare a room for his hoped-for release.

blocks.text: Colossae stood in the region of Phrygia, in the Roman province of Asia, roughly a hundred miles inland from Ephesus. It lay along the Lycus River, a tributary of the Meander, at the foot of the mountains that rise to the south. Ten or eleven miles downstream stood Laodicea, the administrative and banking center of the district, and across the valley stood Hierapolis, famous for its hot springs. The three towns were bound together by trade and by the main road that ran east from the Aegean coast toward the interior.

In earlier centuries Colossae had been a large and wealthy town, known for its wool and for a deep reddish dye that bore its name. By Paul’s day its importance had faded as Laodicea grew, and it had become a modest market town of mixed population. Phrygian natives, Greek settlers, Roman officials, and a sizeable Jewish community lived side by side. The valley was also prone to earthquakes, and a severe one struck the region in the early 60s, damaging Laodicea and very likely Colossae as well.

Paul had not planted the church there in person. Epaphras, a native of Colossae, carried the gospel home, probably during Paul’s long ministry in Ephesus, and he seems to have labored in Laodicea and Hierapolis too. Paul knew the believers by report and through individual contacts, and Philemon was one of those whom he had personally led to Christ. The congregations of the valley met in private homes, and Colossians mentions a church gathering in the house of Nympha as well as the one in Philemon’s house.

The life of such a town shapes the reading of the letter. In a small community everyone would know that Onesimus had fled and that Philemon had suffered loss. The return of the slave would be noticed by neighbors, by fellow slaves in other households, and by the believers who met under Philemon’s roof. Whatever Philemon chose to do would be seen, discussed, and remembered, and it would testify either for or against the gospel that the house church claimed to live by.

Philemon was a man of property. He owned at least one slave and probably several, and his house was large enough to receive a gathering of believers and to offer a guest room to a visiting apostle. Paul calls him a dearly beloved friend and fellow laborer, which suggests that he took an active part in the work of the gospel in his town. Paul also reminds him that he owes his very self to the apostle, a strong hint that Philemon had come to faith through Paul’s own preaching.

Paul’s thanksgiving gives a portrait of his character. Philemon is known for love and faith toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints, and the hearts of the believers have been refreshed through him. The word Paul uses for refreshing describes rest given to the weary, and it suggests hospitality, generosity, and encouragement offered freely. Paul builds his appeal on this reputation. He asks Philemon to do for Onesimus, and through him for Paul, what he had already been doing for so many others.

Apphia, greeted as the sister, was most likely Philemon’s wife. In an ancient household the wife oversaw the domestic staff and the daily running of the home, so any decision about a returning slave would concern her directly. Archippus, called a fellow soldier, may have been their son, though the letter does not say so. Colossians instructs him to fulfill the ministry he had received in the Lord, which suggests that he held some responsibility in the congregation, perhaps in the absence of Epaphras.

The letter is addressed also to the church in Philemon’s house. Early Christians had no buildings set apart for worship, so they met in the homes of members who had space to receive them. A house church might include the owner’s family, slaves and freed persons of the household, neighbors, and friends, and it would share meals together, including the Lord’s Supper. Onesimus would return to a house where master and slave might sit at the same table, and the whole congregation would hear the letter read aloud.

Onesimus was a slave in Philemon’s household. His name, which means useful or profitable, was a common one for slaves, given by owners who hoped their property would live up to it. Paul plays on that meaning when he says that Onesimus was once unprofitable to Philemon and is now profitable to them both. The letter implies that Onesimus had wronged his master in some way, and Paul’s offer to repay anything he owes suggests a financial loss, whether through theft at his departure or through the cost of his absence.

The traditional view is that Onesimus ran away, made his way to Rome, and there came into contact with Paul. Another suggestion holds that he did not intend to escape for good; having offended his master, he may have sought out Paul as a respected friend of the family who could plead for him, a practice that Roman law allowed. The letter does not settle the matter. Either way, Onesimus had placed himself in serious danger, and he came to Paul as a man without standing or security.

In that encounter Onesimus was converted. Paul calls him my son, whom I have begotten in my bonds, using the same family language he uses of Timothy. The change was visible in his conduct, for Onesimus served Paul so faithfully that the apostle wished to keep him. In Colossians he is called a faithful and beloved brother, one of you, and he is entrusted with Tychicus to report on Paul’s affairs. The runaway slave has become a trusted messenger of the churches.

Onesimus’s return home was itself an act of faith. He was going back to a master who had every legal right to punish him, carrying a letter that asked for mercy but could not compel it. Early in the second century a bishop of Ephesus bore the name Onesimus, and some have wondered whether the slave of this letter later rose to that office and helped to gather Paul’s letters, which would explain how so short a note was preserved. The connection cannot be proved, but it is not impossible.

Slavery was woven into every level of Roman society. In the cities of the first century a large share of the population was enslaved, and many more were freed slaves or their children. Slaves worked in fields, mines, and workshops, but also served as household managers, physicians, secretaries, teachers, and business agents. Roman slavery was not based on race. People became slaves through capture in war, through birth to an enslaved mother, through debt, or through being abandoned as infants and raised by traders.

Whatever their work, slaves were legally property. A master could buy, sell, beat, or separate them from their families, and their testimony in court might be taken under torture. Freedom was often granted, especially to household slaves after years of service, and freed persons could rise to wealth and influence. That prospect should not soften the picture. Many slaves lived and died in harsh conditions, and their dignity depended entirely on the character of the one who owned them.

Fugitive slaves faced especially grave penalties. A recaptured runaway could be flogged, branded on the forehead, chained, sold to the mines, or in extreme cases put to death, and anyone who harbored a fugitive could be held liable for the owner’s loss. Professional slave catchers pursued runaways, and owners posted notices offering rewards. Against this background Paul’s letter stands out sharply. Where the law expected punishment, Paul asks that Onesimus be received as Paul himself would be received.

Paul did not launch a campaign to overturn Roman law, which a prisoner writing to a small congregation had no power to do. He did something that reached deeper. He told a master that his slave was now his brother beloved, both in the flesh and in the Lord, and he set their relationship within the fellowship of the church, where there is neither bond nor free. Scripture had long condemned the stealing and selling of human beings, and the gospel declares that every person bears the image of God and that Christ died for slave and master alike.

Such convictions undermine slavery at its root. A man cannot treat as property one whom he must welcome as he would welcome an apostle, and with whom he will share the kingdom forever. The direction of Scripture runs steadily toward freedom, and Paul elsewhere urges slaves to take freedom when it is offered. The letter to Philemon therefore gives no comfort to those who later defended human bondage, and believers who worked to end the slave trade rightly found in its pages a seed of their cause.

The immediate purpose of the letter is plain. Paul is sending Onesimus back, and he asks Philemon to receive him without punishment, to forgive his debt, and to welcome him as a brother in Christ. Paul had the apostolic standing to command what was fitting, yet he chose instead to appeal for love’s sake. He wanted Philemon’s kindness to be freely given, since goodness extracted by pressure would lose its worth. The request is built so that Philemon may act from his own heart.

Paul also had a further hope. He says he would have liked to keep Onesimus with him to serve in Philemon’s place, and he expresses confidence that Philemon will do even more than he asks. Many readers have taken these words as a gentle hint that Philemon might free Onesimus or release him to return to Paul for the work of the gospel. Paul leaves the decision open, yet the direction of his wishes is unmistakable, and the closing mention of his own coming visit adds friendly accountability.

Behind the request lies a larger purpose. Paul wanted the reconciliation of master and slave to display the reconciliation that God has accomplished in Christ. He identifies himself with Onesimus so completely that he asks Philemon to receive the slave as himself and to charge any debt to Paul’s own account. In this the letter mirrors the work of Christ, who takes the sinner’s debt upon Himself and presents the guilty to the Father as accepted in the Beloved.

Finally, Paul wrote for the sake of the church in Philemon’s house. The letter was meant to be read before the gathered believers, and its outcome would shape their understanding of what fellowship in Christ requires. A congregation where a wronged master forgives and embraces a returning slave proclaims the gospel more powerfully than many sermons. Paul’s small letter thus serves a public mission: it calls a whole community to live out the new order of relationships that the cross has created.

Philemon is the shortest of Paul’s letters, only twenty-five verses in the English Bible, and it follows the familiar pattern of ancient correspondence: greeting, thanksgiving, request, and closing. Within that simple frame Paul shows remarkable skill. Words planted in the thanksgiving, such as love, fellowship, heart, refresh, and brother, return later to carry the weight of the appeal. The table below gathers the main facts about the letter, and the comparison that follows sets it beside its companion letter to the same town.

blocks.title: Philemon at a Glance
rows: Author
The apostle Paul, writing as a prisoner of Christ Jesus, with Timothy named in the greeting
Recipients
Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church that met in Philemon’s house at Colossae
Date
Most probably about A.D. 60–62, during Paul’s first Roman imprisonment
Place of writing
Most probably Rome, where Paul lived under guard in rented lodgings
Carriers
Tychicus, accompanied by Onesimus, who also brought the letter to the Colossians
Occasion
The return of Onesimus, a slave who had left Philemon and had been converted through Paul
Main request
That Philemon receive Onesimus as a beloved brother and charge any debt to Paul’s account
Structure
Greeting 1:1-3; thanksgiving 1:4-7; appeal 1:8-20; closing and greetings 1:21-25
Key verses
Central theme
The gospel reconciles people to God and to one another and reshapes every relationship from within

blocks.title: Philemon and Colossians Compared
rows: Addressees
A single household and the congregation meeting in its home
The whole church at Colossae, with greetings to Laodicea
Main concern
Reconciling a master and his returning slave as brothers in Christ
Exalting the supremacy of Christ against a misleading philosophy
Teaching on slavery
Applies the gospel to one particular master and one particular slave
Gives household instructions to slaves and masters, reminding masters that they have a Master in heaven
Shared people
Timothy, Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Luke, Archippus, and Onesimus
The same circle of companions, with Tychicus named as the carrier
Picture of the gospel
Paul takes another’s debt upon himself so that the offender may be received
Christ cancels the record of debt against us by nailing it to His cross

blocks.text: Read together, the two letters show how the truth about Christ becomes the practice of a household. Colossians proclaims that Christ is the image of the invisible God, the head of the church, and the one in whom all things hold together. Philemon shows what that confession means when a master opens his door to the slave who once wronged him. The same Lord who reconciles all things to Himself by the blood of His cross also reconciles a divided home in a small Phrygian town.
